title: Array Sum
description:
Given an integer array, return the sum of all its elements.

### Input
- Line 1: integer `n` — the number of elements.
- Line 2: `n` space-separated integers.

### Output
A single integer: the sum of the array.
editorial:
## Approach
Initialize an accumulator to 0 and add each element. Because you must read every element to know the sum, O(n) time is optimal, and only a single accumulator is needed, giving O(1) extra space.
optimal_explanation: A single pass accumulating a running total is optimal; every element must be read at least once.

import sys

def solve(nums):
    # TODO: return the sum of nums
    return 0

data = sys.stdin.read().split()
n = int(data[0])
nums = list(map(int, data[1:1+n]))
print(solve(nums))

hints: You only need to look at each element once.
Keep a running total as you scan left to right.
Watch out for negative numbers — they reduce the sum.
Sum all elements: `total += a[i]`.

prerequisites.name: Big-O / Complexity Analysis
prerequisites.what: Reasoning about how time and memory grow with the input size.
prerequisites.deep: Big-O bounds the dominant growth term and tells you whether an approach scales to the constraints. Read the limits: n up to 10^5 suggests O(n) or O(n log n), while 10^9 suggests O(log n) or O(1). Sanity-check the work against roughly 10^8 operations per second.
prerequisites.java: No API - this is analysis. Match your algorithm to the constraints stated in each problem before you start coding.
prerequisites.how: The single loop touches each of the n elements once, so the time is Theta(n) - you must read every value to sum it, and no approach is faster.

prerequisites.name: Array Iteration
prerequisites.what: Walking through elements one at a time while maintaining running state such as a sum, max, or counter.
prerequisites.deep: The workhorse of array problems: one for-loop that updates accumulators as it goes. Most linear-time solutions are just one well-chosen pass, so the real skill is deciding what state to carry so a single sweep suffices.
prerequisites.java: Use for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) or for (int x : nums). Prefer a primitive int[] over Integer[] to avoid autoboxing overhead.

prerequisites.name: Integer Overflow (int vs long)

title: Greatest Common Divisor
description:
Compute the greatest common divisor of two non-negative integers.

### Input
Two space-separated integers `a b` on one line.

### Output
gcd(a, b).
editorial:
## Approach
Repeatedly replace (a, b) with (b, a mod b) until b is 0; a is then the gcd.
optimal_explanation: The Euclidean algorithm reduces the arguments logarithmically.

starter_code.python:
a, b = map(int, input().split())

def solve(a, b):
    # TODO: return gcd(a, b)
    return 0

print(solve(a, b))

hints: The Euclidean algorithm is the classic tool.
gcd(a, b) = gcd(b, a mod b).
Recurse/loop until b becomes 0.
When b == 0, the answer is a.

prerequisites.name: Number Theory Basics
prerequisites.what: Divisibility, gcd, and modular arithmetic facts used to reason about integers.
prerequisites.deep: Foundations like the Euclidean algorithm, prime factorization, and modular arithmetic underpin many math problems. Even simple tasks benefit from gcd/lcm identities and knowing how modulo distributes over addition and multiplication.
prerequisites.java: Math.floorMod for correct modulo of negatives; write a short gcd helper (Euclid); BigInteger has gcd() if needed.
prerequisites.how: The gcd is the largest integer dividing both inputs; Euclid's insight is that gcd(a, b) equals gcd(b, a mod b).

prerequisites.name: Recursion
prerequisites.what: A function that calls itself on smaller inputs, with base cases that stop the descent.
prerequisites.deep: Expresses divide-and-conquer and tree/graph walks naturally. Watch the recursion depth against stack limits, and whether subproblems overlap - if they do, add memoization to avoid exponential blow-up.
prerequisites.java: A private static helper that calls itself. The JVM stack handles ~10^4 depth; convert to an explicit ArrayDeque if you risk StackOverflowError.
prerequisites.how: That identity is naturally recursive - recurse on (b, a % b) until the second argument is 0, then a is the answer (a while-loop works too).

prerequisites.name: Modular Reduction
prerequisites.what: Using n % k to wrap indices around and drop redundant whole cycles.
prerequisites.deep: Modulo collapses equivalent states: rotating by k equals rotating by k % n, and hashing or bucketing uses remainders. In Java, beware that % can return a negative result for negative operands.
